Impute
ĭm-pūt´
v. (to reckon to one's account; rendering Hebrew chashab, Greek logizomai)
From Latin imputare, to enter in the reckoning — a bookkeeping word. Scripture's most consequential accounting entries are made with it.

Biblical Definition

To impute is to credit or charge something to an account. Three imputations carry the whole gospel: Adam's sin reckoned to his race, our sin reckoned to Christ, and Christ's righteousness reckoned to us. The pivotal text is Abraham's: “he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness” (Gen 15:6), which Paul presses into a doctrine — “to him that worketh not, but believeth… his faith is counted for righteousness” (Rom 4:5). The blessedness of the man is stated as a negative entry: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin” (Rom 4:8). Nothing is transferred by infusion; everything is transferred by reckoning.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines impute as to charge, to attribute, to set to the account of — and specifically, in theology, to attribute vicariously.

expand to see more

IMPUTE, v.t. To charge; to attribute; to set to the account of; generally ill, sometimes good.

2. To attribute; to ascribe.

3. In theology, to impute is to charge or attribute vicariously; as, the righteousness of Christ is imputed to believers.

Key Scripture

Gen 15:6 — "And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness."

Rom 4:5 — "But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness."

Rom 4:8 — "Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin."

2Co 5:21 — "For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him."

Modern Corruption

Imputation is dismissed as a legal fiction, as though God pretended — when in fact it is the only category that lets a holy God receive sinners without lying about them.

expand to see more

The charge of legal fiction misunderstands what a reckoning is. When a debt is paid by another and the ledger is marked settled, nothing false has been recorded; the account genuinely stands clear because the payment genuinely occurred. 2 Corinthians 5:21 states the double entry with precision: he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. Christ was not made sinful, nor are we made intrinsically righteous — the reckoning is real because the substitution was real.

Where the doctrine is lost, sanctification is immediately corrupted, because the believer starts trying to establish the standing he has already been given. Imputed righteousness is the ground a Christian stands on while he is being made holy; delete it and holiness becomes the anxious manufacture of a standing, which Scripture calls going about to establish their own righteousness (Rom 10:3).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chashab (H2803), to reckon, to account; Greek logizomai (G3049), to count up, put to one's account — used eleven times in Romans 4 alone.

expand to see more

Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to reckon, impute; Genesis 15:6, counted to him for righteousness.

Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, credit; Romans 4:3-11, 2 Corinthians 5:19, not imputing their trespasses.

Greek ellogeo (G1677) — to charge to an account; Philemon 18, put that on mine account.

Usage

"“He counted it to him for righteousness” — the entry that founds the doctrine."

"“Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin” — blessedness as an accounting negative."

"“Put that on mine account” — Paul enacts imputation for a runaway slave."
